title: Exploring Diffusion Transformer Designs via Grafting

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims that “all tested hybrid designs achieve excellent quality (FID: 2.15–2.38 vs. 2.27 for DiT-XL/2)” and that grafting “consistently outperforms the baseline across all replacement ratios and operator types.” Table 4 contains no FID of 2.15, reports many viable hybrid FIDs above 2.38 (e.g., 2.53–3.69 and 8.23), and the baseline FID of 2.27 is better than every reported successful hybrid result. Several 100%-replacement variants are marked as poor generation/FID > 50.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, statement that grafting “consistently outperforms the baseline across all replacement ratios and operator types”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: FID is lower-is-better, and Table 4's baseline is 2.27. The best listed hybrid FID is 2.37 (MLP r=6 at 75% replacement), while the remaining hybrid results are worse, often dramatically so. Thus the reported results do not merely fail to establish universal improvement; they directly contradict it.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.3, paragraph beginning “Full self-grafting with 10% data achieves near-baseline performance”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states that full MHA self-grafting with 10% data achieves “an FID of 2.53 vs. 2.27 for the baseline.” Table 2, the cited result table, reports FID = 2.49 for the 0.63% Stage-1 / 10.0% Stage-2 MHA self-grafting condition.

The body text says that at k=32 “all 28 layers exhibit L_k > 0.7, with 22 layers exceeding 0.85.” The Figure 2 caption instead says that at k=32 “15 out of 28 layers exhibit values exceeding 0.5.” If all 28 exceeded 0.7, all 28 necessarily would exceed 0.5; both descriptions cannot characterize the same plotted measurement.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.4, conclusion that attention locality “justifies replacing MHA with local operators in all layers”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This conclusion is contradicted by the paper's own experiments. The same section states that replacing all MHA layers with sliding-window attention degrades FID from 2.27 to 53.9. Table 4 likewise shows severe failure or degradation at 100% MHA replacement. The evidence supports selective/interleaved replacement, not replacement in all layers.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2, MHA results bullet “Replacement strategy: Interleaved vs. Full”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims that at 100% replacement “performance sharply degrades (all FIDs > 75).” Table 4 reports Hyena-SE at 100% MHA replacement with FID = 8.23, which is poor relative to baseline but plainly not greater than 75.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 Stage-1 setup versus Appendix Table C.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.1 says each replacement operator is initialized with “an initial learning rate of 1e-4.” Appendix Table C.1, presented as the hyperparameters for the same DiT-XL/2 hybrid grafting experiments, gives the Stage-1 initial learning rate as 1 × 10^-3. These are a tenfold discrepancy in a central training hyperparameter.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5 Results, Table 5 caption, and Abstract speedup claim for PixArt-Σ
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The 50% Hyena-X row in Table 5 reports baseline latency 235.46 ms and grafted latency 148.32 ms. Their ratio is 235.46/148.32 = 1.588, matching the table cell's 1.59×, not the repeatedly claimed 1.43× speedup. The Section 5 text, Table 5 caption, abstract, and conclusion all report 1.43× without supplying another measurement or calculation that yields that value.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Section 5 claim of “less than a 2% drop in GenEval score”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The reported overall scores are 49.75 for baseline and 47.78 for the 50% grafted model. This is a 1.97-point difference but a relative decrease of approximately 3.96% ((49.75-47.78)/49.75). Calling it a “<2% drop” is incorrect unless explicitly described as percentage points; the paper instead uses percent terminology. Moreover, the initial comparison uses different samplers (50-step DDPM for baseline versus 20-step DPM-Solver for grafted), making it unsuitable as an architecture-only quality comparison.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5 Results, baseline-versus-grafted PixArt-Σ quality comparison
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The headline GenEval comparison contrasts a baseline evaluated using “50-step DDPM sampling for maximum quality” with a grafted model evaluated using “20-step DPM Solver for efficiency.” Since sampler and number of denoising steps differ, the 49.75 versus 47.78 comparison confounds architectural modification with inference procedure. The later matched-20-step comparison is the relevant comparison, but it is not the basis of the abstract's claimed quality drop.

The paper claims the 14-layer depth-to-width model “surpasses even the original DiT-XL/2 (FID=2.27) when evaluated on a held-out test set” and that this proves parallel architectures are “universally superior.” Table 6 reports the grafted model's FID as 2.77, worse than DiT-XL/2's 2.27, and contains no held-out-test result showing the claimed reversal. The reported comparison only supports improvement over some lower-depth baselines, not superiority to the original or universal architectural superiority.

The conclusion says grafting “completely solves the problem of architecture design,” enables “any architectural idea with negligible compute,” and “universally outperforms training from scratch across all tasks, modalities, and model scales.” These claims are unsupported and contradicted by the paper's own limitations: it studies principally MHA/MLP replacement, requires a pretrained model, has full-replacement failures, reports quality loss in several settings, and tests only a small set of models/tasks. The reported experiments cannot establish universality or complete solution of architecture design.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction footnote 1, attribution to Goldschmidt et al. [4]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [4] is Eliezer Goldschmidt's 2014 plant-biology article, “Plant grafting: New mechanisms, evolutionary implications.” The footnote asserts that Goldschmidt “has shown that the principles of biological grafting ... can be directly applied to neural network architectures” and provides a theoretical foundation for activation transfer. A 2014 plant-grafting paper cannot have demonstrated neural-network activation transfer; this is a fabricated or grossly misrepresented attribution.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A, final sentence on Shen et al. [52]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says Shen et al. [52] “introduced the concept of ‘activation distillation’ for operator replacement in diffusion models.” Reference [52] is the 2021 AAAI paper “Progressive network grafting for few-shot knowledge distillation,” predating modern diffusion-transformer work and not a paper on operator replacement in diffusion models. The citation may be relevant to network grafting/distillation generally, but it does not support the claimed diffusion-model-specific attribution.

Section E.1 explicitly says Figure E.1 shows activation distributions for representative PixArt-Σ layers, but the caption ends with “Model: DiT-XL/2 Layer.” The figure is therefore mislabeled or its described model is inconsistent with the surrounding PixArt-Σ experiment.
